en: The *Buddhastotra in One Hundred and Fifty Verses*,
composed by the Venerable Mātrceṭa;
translated by the Da Tang Śramaṇa Yijing at Nālandā Monastery.
The World-Honored One is most supreme; He has skillfully severed all seeds of delusion.
Immeasurable and excellent merits are fully gathered within the Tathāgata’s body.
Only the Buddha is worthy of refuge, worthy of praise, and worthy of service.
Those who contemplate according to the truth should dwell within this teaching.
The Lord of the World has already eliminated all evil afflictions and habitual tendencies;
with both merit and wisdom perfected, only the Venerable One remains, never to decline.
Even if one should give rise to evil views and harbor resentment toward the Honored One,
searching for faults in his physical or verbal actions, they would find no vulnerability.
He prophesied that I would obtain a human body and, upon hearing the Dharma, would give rise to joy.
Just as a blind turtle in the vast ocean might encounter a floating log with a single hole,
so too do I— whose mindfulness is ever-failing and who has fallen into a deep pit due to delusions and karma—
use these words to praise the Buddha’s true merits.
The Sage’s sphere is immeasurable, his noble virtues are boundless;
for the sake of seeking my own benefit, I now praise but a small portion of them.
Homage to the Teacherless Wisdom, whose nature is composed of rare and wondrous qualities.
Who can know the measure of his merit, wisdom, and majestic radiance?
The virtues of the Tathāgata are limitless; they are peerless and beyond description.
Now, seeking blessings and well-being, I shall offer praise through these words and names.
My power of wisdom is slight and shallow, while the Buddha’s virtue is boundless;
I pray only that you, with great compassion, rescue me who have no place of refuge.
To enemies and kin you are entirely impartial, giving rise to great compassion without cause.
Throughout the entire realm of sentient beings, you always act as a true and virtuous friend.
You are even able to renounce your inner wealth, let alone your external possessions;
being free from any heart of stinginess, you fulfill the wishes of all who seek.
He protected their bodies with his own body, and ransomed their lives with his own life;
he saved a single pigeon at the cost of his entire frame, rejoicing without a trace of stinginess.
The Honored One feared not the evil realms, nor did he crave the happy destinies.
Only when the mind is pure and clear does ethical discipline (śīla) thereby become perfected.
Always remaining free from all crookedness and always associating with those who are upright,
one realizes that the intrinsic nature of all karmic actions is empty, abiding solely in the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
When the multitude of sufferings press upon his body, the Honored One is able to remain well-composed in contemplation;
with right wisdom he cuts off all delusions, and toward those who have transgressed, he gives rise to universal compassion.
Sacrificing his own life to rescue others from distress, he gives birth to immeasurable joy.
Like one who has suddenly revived from death, this joy exceeds that [previous state].
Though an enemy harms their body and constantly torments them at all times,
one does not contemplate their faults or evils, but always gives rise to a heart of great compassion.
The seed of perfect, universal enlightenment is that which the mind constantly cherishes;
the Great Hero’s invincible wisdom is such that none can equal it.
Of the peerless fruit of enlightenment, ascetic practice is the cause.
Because of this, disregarding one's own body, one diligently cultivates all supreme qualities.
Whether toward the noble and wealthy or the poor and lowly, one induces great compassion equally;
amidst all such distinctions, there is no thought of high or low.
The fruit of the samādhi of supreme bliss is a mind free from attachment,
universally saving all sentient beings with uninterrupted great compassion.
Though the Honored One encountered extreme suffering, he did not long for pleasure.
The various merits of sublime wisdom are peerless and unsurpassed.
Amidst the diverse phenomena of defilement and purity, one discerns the false to extract the true;
like the king of swans, one drinks the milk and leaves behind the water.
Throughout immeasurable billions of kalpas, you have courageously pursued bodhi;
in every birth therein, you sacrificed your body to seek the sublime Dharma.
For the duration of three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you were diligent and never weary.
Holding this as one’s supreme companion, one realizes wondrous Bodhi.
The Honored One is free from a jealous or envious mind; toward those who are inferior, he eliminates thoughts of contempt.
Being impartial and free from strife, his sublime practices are all perfectly accomplished.
The Honored One values only the practice of causes, not seeking the perfection of the resultant stage;
by universally cultivating all superior deeds, all virtues naturally reach fulfillment.
Diligently practicing the dharma of renunciation, one transcends and ascends to the pinnacle of all practices.
Whether sitting, lying down, or walking, there is no place that is not a supreme field of merit.
It eradicates all defilements of transgression and increases pure virtues;
this is accomplished through the accumulation of practice, and thus the Honored One alone is most unsurpassed.
All blessings are perfectly fulfilled, And every fault is entirely eliminated;
The Tathāgata’s pure Dharma-body Has severed all habitual tendencies.
Accumulating and further accumulating the provisions, The merit returns to the body of the Tamer.
Seeking a simile for comparison, none can equal the Buddha.
Surveying all the worlds, one finds many calamities, obstacles, and afflictions;
even if there were a small portion of goodness, it would be easy to find a counterpart.
Far removed from all faults and afflictions, Serene, peaceful, and unmoving—
The most supreme roots of goodness Admit of no comparison.
The Tathāgata’s wisdom is profound and far-reaching, Bottomless and without limit.
Worldly affairs are likened to the Buddha’s body, As a cow’s footprint compared to the great ocean.
His profound benevolence sustains all beings; In the world, there is nothing to compare with it.
The great earth bears heavy burdens, Yet compared to this, it is truly light.
The darkness of ignorance has been dispelled; the light of the Muni shines everywhere.
Worldly wisdom cannot serve as a simile, like a firefly before the light of the sun.
The three karmas of the Tathāgata are pure, like the bright autumn moon over a clear pool.
The world’s purity is likened to the Buddha’s body, yet both share the nature of becoming defiled dust.
All such superior matters cited above from within the world are utterly surpassed by the Buddha-dharma; worldly affairs are truly pitiable.
The precious collection of the noble Dharma has the Buddha at its summit;
among those that are unsurpassed and peerless, only Buddhas are equal to Buddhas.
From the ocean of the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom, I shall now praise but a small portion according to my inclination.
With these humble words I praise your supreme virtues; before you, I am truly filled with shame.
When worldly folk behold your subduing of Māra, they all submit and bow in reverence;
yet when I contemplate that [subjugation] as being identical to true nature, I consider it equal to a light feather.
Even if there were a great battle array, where wisdom and valor could crush and subdue it, the Sage’s virtue transcends the world; thus, subduing those [demons] is not even a fit metaphor.
Immediately following the subduing of Māra, during the final watch of the night,
Having severed all habitual tendencies of affliction, his supreme virtues are entirely perfected.
With noble wisdom he dispels the manifold darkness, surpassing the light of a thousand suns;
he subdues all heterodox schools—rare indeed, with none able to equal him.
The three roots of goodness are perfected; greed, anger, and delusion are forever extinguished.
All seeds and habitual tendencies have been entirely eliminated; this purity is beyond compare.
The Honored One of the Sublime Dharma constantly praises it, while he always censures that which is not the True Dharma.
Regarding these points of the heterodox and the orthodox, his mind harbors neither hatred nor affection.
Toward the assembly of noble disciples as well as the teachers and followers of external paths—
amidst such opposition and compliance— the Buddha’s mind has from the beginning been without duality.
The mind has no attachment to virtues, nor is there any craving for them;
how excellent is this utter stainlessness! Noble wisdom is ever perfectly pure.
The faculties are perpetually serene and still, forever free from the deluded mind.
Within all objective realms, direct perception arises from personal observation.
Through mindfulness and wisdom, one exhausts the limit of reality; this is beyond the comprehension of the foolish and ignorant.
Skillfully establishing linguistic conventions, one realizes that state where words have ceased.
Tranquil and unimpeded light, pure and bright beyond compare,
With wondrous form rare in the world— who would not harbor a heart of reverence?
Whether one gazes upon it for a brief moment, Or beholds it constantly, [one is moved].
The wondrous marks are never dual; from beginning to end, all are equally joyful.
With a body of supreme majesty and virtue, those who behold it never grow weary;
even after passing through immeasurable eons, their admiration remains as fresh as at the first sight.
The essential nature of the supported virtues and the mind of the supporting virtues—both in their nature and characteristics—are fused;
subject and object were never distinct from the beginning.
Such virtues of the Sugata are all gathered within the person of the Tathāgata.
Apart from the Buddha’s body adorned with the marks and signs, there is no other place of peace.
By virtue of the merit of my past lives, I have fortunately encountered the Teacher, the Tamer;
I look up and praise this mountain of merit, far repaying the prediction bestowed by the Honored One.
All classes of sentient beings are sustained by afflictions;
only the Buddha can skillfully remove them, for he dwells long in the world out of compassion.
To whom, then, should one first pay homage? Only to the Buddha, the Honored One of Great Compassion.
Your holy virtue transcends the world, yet out of compassionate vows you dwell within birth and death.
While the Honored One abides in the bliss of tranquility, you remain amidst the turbid world for the sake of all beings;
through eons of long-drawn diligent effort, you have cultivated a heart of loving-kindness for the sake of all.
Returning from the ultimate truth to benefit the mundane world, they are impelled by great compassion;
like a spell that summons a hidden dragon, they raise clouds and pour down sweet rain.
Constantly abiding in the supreme state of certainty, they regard enemies and kin with equal vision.
A person of fierce and reckless clamor has cast himself under the protection of holy virtue.
With the lion’s roar of supernormal power, he proclaims himself the Honored One of the Three Realms;
though long since weary of fame and renown, he praises himself out of compassion.
Constantly practicing for the benefit of others, you have never harbored a thought for self-interest;
your compassionate mindfulness extends to all sentient beings, while you feel no partial attachment to yourself.
Your vows of compassion are boundless as you transform the multitudes according to their capacities.
Benefiting all wherever one goes, like scattering sacrificial food;

With a profound mind mindful of all beings, never abandoning them for even a moment— If, while benefiting others, one instead encounters humiliation, The fault lies elsewhere; it is not the Buddha’s doing.
With a compassionate voice, you expound the wondrous meaning; it is truthful and not spoken in vain.
Whether extensive or concise, it accords with the capacities of beings; the provisional and the ultimate turn according to the times.
If one hears your venerable exposition, who would not marvel at its rarity?
Even if they harbor malicious intent, those with wisdom will all place their faith in them.
Their words of meaning are always skillful; even if they occasionally utter coarse speech, the benefit it brings is never in vain, and thus it all becomes truly wondrous.
Whether gentle or coarse, he transforms sentient beings according to their needs;
with the unimpeded mind of noble wisdom, all things are equalized in a single flavor.
Victorious is this stainless karma, as skillful as a master craftsman.
Having attained this subtle and wondrous body, he utters these precious verses.
All who behold him rejoice; all who hear his teaching find their minds opened.
With a beautiful countenance he proclaims sublime words, like the moon pouring forth nectar.
The compassionate clouds dispense the rain of Dharma, capable of purifying the dust of defiled desires;
like that king of golden-winged birds, they swallow and destroy the venom of all dragons;
they can utterly extinguish the darkness of ignorance, comparable to the light of a thousand suns.
Crushing the mountain of self-conceit is like the vajra-pestle of the Lord of Devas;
realizing the truth through direct experience is free from error. Through meditative concentration, one eliminates the distracted mind;
by practicing well according to reality, all three matters are brought to perfection.
Having first heard what the Buddha taught, my mind was gladdened and enlightened;
from this point on, through right reflection, I have eliminated all defilements.
I am able to comfort those who suffer and inspire fear in those who are heedless.
To those attached to pleasure, he exhorts them toward renunciation; according to their circumstances, he guides and inspires them all.
Those of superior wisdom realize the joy of the Dharma; those of middling faculties give rise to resolute conviction;
the shallow and inferior develop faith. Thus, the Honored One’s words universally bring benefit.
Skillfully uprooting all false views, you lead beings toward Nirvana;
you are able to wash away the stains of sin, for the Honored One has let fall the rain of Dharma.
With omniscience free from obstruction, you dwell perpetually in right mindfulness.
The predictions made by the Tathāgata are invariably free from error.
There is no place or time that is unsuitable, nor does he ever turn [the wheel of Dharma] for those who are not fit vessels.
The words of the Honored One are never uttered in vain; all who hear them shall diligently practice.
This supreme path of skillful means is free from admixture and can be practiced;
it is virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end, qualities found in no other teaching.
Because it is thus exclusively wholesome, the mad and foolish give rise to a mind of slander.
If one feels aversion toward this teaching, there is no such resentment among those [who follow it].
Throughout kalpas as a deluded mass, one has fully experienced all manner of bitter poisons;
even if this teaching were not good, one should still practice the recollection of the Buddha.
How much more so when one can bring great benefit and further proclaim the profound and wondrous meaning;
even if one's head were to be consumed by fire, one should first rescue this teaching.
The bliss of sovereign enlightenment is eternally serene through the virtue of the Sage.
All arise from this teaching, realizing that state beyond words.
The true teaching of the Hero of the World causes all heterodox sects to tremble with fear;
the Mara King harbors a mind of affliction, while gods and humans give rise to supreme joy.
The great earth is without discrimination, Equally able to support all;
The holy teaching benefits all beings, With both the heterodox and the orthodox receiving its grace.
Upon briefly hearing what the Buddha has taught, One becomes established in the Vajra lineage.
Though one has not yet escaped the cage of worldly confinement, one will ultimately transcend the realm of death.
Hearing the Dharma, one contemplates its meaning; practicing it well according to reality, the three levels of wisdom become perfected. Among other teachings, none possess this.
Only the Bull-King Sage, who perfectly accords with the wondrous and perfect principle, taught this doctrine;
if one does not diligently practice it, what resentment could be greater than this?
Hearing it but briefly removes thirst and craving, and even those with false views give rise to faith.
Those who hear it give rise to a joyful mind, And by relying on this, they fully possess the pure precepts.
His birth was met with universal joy at the time, And his growth brought delight to the entire world.
His great transformation benefited all living beings, And his demonstration of extinction gave rise to sorrowful feelings.
Chanting praises dispels all poisons; mindfulness invites joy and celebration;
seeking it awakens the light of wisdom; and through realization, the mind becomes perfectly pure.
Those who encounter it are made noble, and by serving it with reverence, a superior spirit arises.
Serving him brings about the causes for merit; personally attending him removes sorrow and suffering.
His ethical discipline (*śīla*) is pure and pristine; his meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is tranquil and serene;
his wisdom (*prajñā*) is perfected and harmoniously integrated—the accumulation of blessings as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
The Blessed One’s form, his teaching, and the Dharma he has realized—
among all that is seen, heard, thought, or known, these jewels are most supreme.
They serve as an island for those drifting in the ocean, and they provide constant protection against harm to oneself.
To those who fear, he provides refuge and leads them to liberation.
Through pure precepts, one becomes a wondrous vessel; as a fertile field, one produces excellent fruit.
A virtuous friend is able to bring great benefit, and through him, the life of wisdom is perfected.
Practicing kindness, harmony, and patience, all who see them rejoice;
by extensively gathering a heart of benevolence and compassion, their merit becomes boundless.
Free from faults in body and speech, love and respect arise because of this.
All auspicious benefits and purposes depend entirely upon the virtues of the Sugata.

The Guide is able to provide excellent guidance; he inspires diligence in those who have fallen into arrogance, and through meditative concentration, he tames the crooked mind so that those lost on the path return to the true way.
Those whose roots of goodness are matured, he guides by means of the three vehicles;
as for those who are stubborn and unruly, he temporarily sets them aside out of compassion.
Toward those who encounter calamity, he provides relief and encourages them to practice virtue.
Compassionate toward suffering sentient beings, you bring benefit and joy to all classes of living things.
You give rise to thoughts of loving-kindness toward those who harm you; you feel sorrow for those who have lost their practice;
and you arouse compassion for the violent and cruel—your holy virtue is beyond praise.
His kindness is as boundless as the heavens, known by all throughout the world;
yet toward those who respond with resentment, the Honored One ever gives rise to compassion.
Sacrificing his own body to save all beings, he feels no anxiety regarding his personal affairs.
For those who have fallen away, you personally provide protection;
practicing acts of kindness throughout two lifetimes, you transcend all worlds.
Always illuminating the darkness, the Venerable One is the wick of the lamp of wisdom.
The enjoyments experienced by humans and devas differ according to their respective types;
yet the flavor of the Honored One’s True Dharma alone is equal and without distinction.
It does not regard lineage, physical strength, or youthful bloom.
Whosoever possesses roots of goodness, All who seek shall find their fulfillment.
He extensively manifests various wonders; Arising great compassion without a specific cause, The assembly of sages, humans, and devas, Join their palms and all draw near.
Alas! The fear of birth and death—only with the appearance of a Buddha does it shine forth.
He benefits all sentient beings and is able to fulfill their every wish.
To dwell together with evil people is to destroy one's joy and take on sorrow and peril.
Though slandered, afflicted, and harmed, he received it as if it were supreme merit;
for the sake of sentient beings, he practiced with diligent toil, yet never possessed a mind of attachment.
The World-Honored One’s rare virtues are difficult to express in words.
The Honored One traveled through perilous and evil paths; Through the horse-barley and the ox-yoke, he practiced austerities for six years, Accepting them with composure and without retreat.
Now dwelling in the most supreme position, He compassionately transforms all living beings.
Even when encountering those who are contemptuous, one’s physical and verbal conduct remains exceedingly humble and respectful;
even toward those of high station and noble masters, one never harbors a mind of arrogance.
One subjects oneself to serve all sentient beings, being as lowly and reverent as a servant.
The capacities and emotions of beings number in the millions; The points of debate and difficulty reach hundreds of thousands.
With the Tathāgata’s compassionate and kind voice, A single answer severs every doubt.
His kindness is deeper than heaven and earth; Yet some turn their backs on this virtue and give rise to deep resentment.
The World-Honored One regards the ultimate limit of enmity as if it were the greatest kindness.
When the enemy turns even more harmful toward him, the World-Honored One turns even more affectionate toward that enemy.
While they constantly seek out the Buddha’s faults, the Buddha regards them with gratitude.
Invited by the jealousy of heterodox sects, Poisoned rice and fiery pits were offered;
Through his compassionate vows, they were transformed into a clear pond, And the poison was changed into nectar.
With patience he subdued their rage, And with mantras he dissolved their slander.
The power of compassion subdues demonic enmity; right wisdom overcomes perverse poison.
For eons upon eons, the masses have wandered in delusion, habituating themselves to evil until it became their very nature;
yet through the Perfect and Wondrous Conduct of the Honored One alone, a single thought can overturn it and transform it into goodness.
Gentleness subdues violence, generosity breaks stinginess and greed,
and kind speech overcomes harsh words— these alone are the supreme skillful means of the Honored One.
Nanda subdued his great pride, and Aṅgulimāla gave rise to a heart of compassion.
Who would not praise this rarity: that those difficult to tame can be well-tamed?
Only the Noble Disciples of the World-Honored One find delight in the flavor of the Dharma;
they take comfort in a seat of grass, for a golden couch is not what they prize.
Skillfully knowing the faculties, desires, and natures [of beings], he gathers and transforms them according to their capacities and conditions;
sometimes he awaits their request, and sometimes he speaks of his own accord without being asked.
Initially he expounds on generosity, morality, and so forth, whereby the mind gradually becomes purified.
Thereafter, he expounded the Dharma of ultimate reality, leading all to its final and perfect realization.
In this place of fearful drifting, only the Buddha is worthy of refuge;
the courageous and Greatly Compassionate Honored One rescues all living beings.
Bodies like clouds pervade the Dharma-realm; the rain of Dharma falls upon the lands of dust.
Manifestations appear each different, varying according to the capacities of beings.
Utterly pure and free from conflict, you alone, O Honored One, are worthy of veneration.
Extensively benefiting all humans and devas, all should offer them worship.
With body and speech free from active fabrication, they skillfully transform all regions;
their teachings are wondrously harmonious—such virtue belongs only to the Honored One.
Having long cultivated the purity of the three karmas, infinite and wondrous omens have appeared;
yet throughout all the worlds, never before has such supreme virtue been seen.
How much more so for one who, toward those of extreme evil, practices only the highest compassion!
Extensively benefiting all sentient beings with courageous and diligent vigor,
those śrāvakas who know the Dharma and constantly serve the Honored One—
even if they were to realize nirvāṇa— would ultimately still be called "indebted."
Those noble ones who train for their own sake alone,
having abandoned the mind that benefits living beings, are not called those who repay their debt.
Having awakened from the sleep of ignorance, they survey all directions with compassion.
Bearing this burden with uplifted diligence, one should draw near to the Noble and Good.
When Māra and his enemies raise affliction and harm, the Buddha’s power has already been able to eliminate them;
among his fearless merits, this reveals but a small portion.
With a compassionate heart transforming all, the Noble One’s intent is free from seeking;
there is no benefit or joy he does not bestow, for his enlightened deeds are thus complete.
If even the Tathāgata’s supreme and wondrous Dharma could ever be shifted or altered, [then so might this].
Devadatta and Sunakṣatra should not have been cast into this teaching.
Throughout the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, they have repeatedly harmed one another;
it is for this reason that the Buddha appeared in the world to reveal the truth and transform sentient beings.
At the Deer Park, you delivered Kūṭadanta; in the Forest of Firmness, you transformed Subhadra.
Now that the roots and conditions for this land are exhausted, no further karmic debts remain to bind you.
For long you have turned the Wheel of Dharma, awakening all those lost in delusion.
Disciples as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, All capable of benefiting the three realms of existence;
By means of the supreme Vajra-samādhi, They shatter their own firm bodies,
Yet without abandoning great compassion, They manifest emanations throughout all directions.
Having perfected the practices for the dual benefit of self and others, you have completed both the form-body and the dharma-body;
you rescue and gather even the icchantikas, manifesting the Buddha-nature at the twin śāla trees.
Your compassionate heart penetrates the three realms of existence, and your physical manifestations respond to all quarters.
By dividing his body into grains of millet, he then dwelt in perfect stillness (*parinirvāṇa*).
How wonderful is this extraordinary conduct! This body of rare merit and the great awakening’s various Dharma-gates have never before existed in the world.
The flow of your grace pervades all sentient beings, while your body and speech remain eternally tranquil;
yet the ignorant and foolish turn their backs on the Sage’s kindness, giving rise to slander and anger toward you.
Your treasury of the Dharma-jewels is truly boundless, and the source of your virtue and ocean of merit are indeed immeasurable.
If there are sentient beings who have once paid homage to the Honored One, To pay homage to him is likewise called "proper homage.
The holy virtues and divine merits are inexhaustible; My present wisdom is inferior, like a speck of dust.
Desiring to praise the mountain of the Tathāgata’s merit, I am struck with fear at its precipice and withdraw; for this reason, I desist.
The realms are immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless; the principles are inconceivable, difficult to see, and difficult to realize.
Only the noble wisdom of the Buddha alone understands them; how could they be praised by the ignorant and foolish?
Each single hair-pore and each mark suffuses the Dharma-realm; Each single practice and each virtue pervades the source of the mind.
Pure and vast, like a fragrant pool, It can heal the thirst of sentient beings' afflictions.
I praise the ocean of the Muni’s virtues; by this wholesome karma, may I proceed toward Bodhi.
May all sentient beings universally give rise to the supreme mind, forever leaving behind the deluded and false consciousness of the mundane and ignorant.
The Hymn in One Hundred and Fifty Verses in Praise of the Buddha (Buddhastotra)
